SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology04 / 20
1. Symbolic Interactionism and Microsociology

Microsociology focuses on social interactions at the interpersonal level

Social Interaction: the ways in which people respond to one another, whether physical or virtual (NOTE: per the definition, absence of interaction is a particular type of interaction).

Microsociology is often synonymous with the symbolic interactionism perspective.

If you view the world from the perspective of symbolic interactionism, you are conducting microsociological analysis

If you want to study social interactions at the interpersonal level, you will in some way take a perspective of symbolic interactionism

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology05 / 20
1. Symbolic Interactionism and Microsociology

Three tenets of the symbolic interactionism perspective (Blumer 1969):

Human beings act towards things based on the meanings those things have for them;

Such ascribed meanings of things arise out of the interaction of the individual with others;

The meanings are interpreted by people in specific contexts.

“human beings interpret or ‘define’ each other’s actions instead of merely reacting to each other’s action.’’

------Herbert Blumer (1900-1987)

What matters is NOT what it is (i.e., the essence), but what it is perceived to be (i.e., interpretation)!

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology06 / 20
2. Microsociological Approaches: a. The social construction of reality theory

The Social Construction of Reality Theory (Berger and Luckmann’s, 1966)

Reality is not absolute, and what we understand to be "real" is actually a social construct.

A social construct is a “reality” created by people in the process of social interaction through attaching meanings and interpreting symbols.

The theory was developed based on the Thomas Theorem: “If men define situations as real, they are real in their consequences.” ---William Isaac Thomas (1863-1947)

The theory is Descriptive (i.e., “is/are”), not Normative (i.e., “ought to be”)

An Examples illustrating the Thomas Theorem:

A prisoner attacked people mumbling absent mindedly to themselves. To the deranged inmate, these lip movements were curses or insults. No matter that they weren’t; the results were the same.

What do you see?

What if that person is Joshua David Bell?

an American Grammy Award-winning violinist who has performed with many of the world's major orchestras and conductors.

What would happen if he plays one of the most difficult pieces ever written on a violin worth $3.5 million?

What matters is NOT the essence, but interpretations.

Joshua Bell played one of the most difficult pieces ever written on a violin worth $3.5 million dollars at a subway station. In total, Bell played for about 45 minutes to about 1,100 people moving through the station. During this time, only a handful stopped to listen; he collected $32.

2. Microsociological Approaches: a. The social construction of reality theory

Implication:

Definition of situation is important!

E.g.: The Slow Elevator

Sarah is the manager of an office building, and the tenants are complaining about the elevator. It’s old and slow, and they have to wait a lot. Several tenants are threatening to break their leases if the management company don’t fix the problem. Please help Sarah to find a solution.

Sarah eventually developed a solution that is extremely cheap and effective by re-defining the problem. Do you know what she did?

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology14 / 20
2. Microsociological Approaches: a. The social construction of reality theory

Can people construct or interpret meanings as they want?

A Joke:

Allen (a bank robber), walks up to the teller and hands her a note that reads. “I have a gun. Give me all your cash.”

The teller, however, is puzzled, because he reads “I have a gub.” “No, it’s gun”, Allen says.

“Looks like ‘gub’ to me.” the teller says, then asks another teller to help him read the note, then another, and finally everyone is arguing over what the note means.

Allen did not succeed in robbing the bank ...

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology15 / 20
2. Microsociological Approaches: a. The social construction of reality theory

It is NOT a solo game, but a social process!

They rely on tacit agreement from all parties of interaction; In other words, people should be on the same page.

If the definitions of situation from all sides of interaction do not line up, the interaction process would yield a “reality” that is not intended or within expectation (i.e., a crisis situation).

The ability to define the situation reflects a person’s (or, a group’s) influences and/or power within society.

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology17 / 20
2. Microsociological Approaches: a. The social construction of reality theory

Not only “situation”, but also “self”, are interactively constructed.

The “looking glass self”: a term coined by Charles H. Cooley to refer to the fact that our sense of self is based on our perception of other’s perception of us. In other words, the self is “living in the minds of others”

Inter-subjectivity: we are acting based on our perceptions of other’s perceptions of us (i.e. self-view, or sense of self)

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology20 / 20
Slide 20

Impression Management: A process by which people attempt to control how others perceive/define them in order to create a desired “reality” (e.g., compel others to react to them in the ways they wish).

A purposeful effort to “define the situation”.

A natural consequence of the “looking glass self”
